summary:
No department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding was located for Boyacá. A visitor to the department is therefore assessed against Colombia's national framework and the national pattern of anti-trans violence, with incidents from other departments cited only as evidence of how that pattern expresses itself.

Colombia's formal legal framework is among the most developed in Latin America, and it governs Boyacá. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

The violence against trans Colombians is lethal and documented. On 5 April 2025 a 28-second video went viral showing Sara Millerey, 32, flailing in a creek in Bello, Antioquia, unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands; she died of a second cardiac arrest at three the following afternoon. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation, police interrogated local residents, and no one has been arrested. Solidarity events were held in several cities to denounce transphobia. Thirteen trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023. Reporting on earlier fatal attacks recalls gay men lured through an app and killed, a trans rough-sleeper stabbed while sleeping, and people killed in their homes and in a hairdresser.

Some of the targeting is organised. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, flyer campaigns distributed on streets and via WhatsApp name "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a campaign run by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. Three armed men told trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, she had one week to leave town or be killed; after hiding for a week she fled at night. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024. Discrimination confines trans women in Caquetá mainly to hairdressing or sex work.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to facilities and custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.
tangentialFactors:
The absence of Boyacá-specific reporting is itself a limit on the assessment. Every incident located in the inventory occurred in other departments: Bello and Antioquia for the Millerey killing, Caquetá for the social cleansing campaigns, Guajira for the posted kill list. Whether comparable organised campaigns are running inside Boyacá is not established either way by the available sources.

Enforcement examples come from elsewhere in the country and show the machinery working unevenly. The Attorney General's Office has counted LGBTI murders nationally, the police interrogated local residents in Bello without making an arrest, and the constitutional rulings protecting entry to premises arose from a hotel, a shopping mall in Cali and a boardwalk in Santa Marta. Institutional reach therefore exists on paper and in some recorded cases, but conviction for the transphobic killing recorded in April 2025 remained outstanding months later.

The national totals sit alongside each other without reconciling: 41 trans women killed in 2023, 8 between February and April 2024, 13 trans people in the first quarter of 2025, and 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025. Different counting bodies and categories produce figures that cannot be added together, but each independently indicates a sustained rate of killing.

Conflict dynamics shape the threat. The flyer campaigns in Guajira and Caquetá are attributed to armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement, and the Special Jurisdiction for Peace processed the violence as gender persecution arising from the conflict. Boyacá's own conflict history is not addressed in the inventory.
localsOnly:
Resident trans Colombians change the sex marker on identification by signing a document before a notary, a route open since June 2015 without judicial examination or psychiatric assessment, and national documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 grounds recognition in self-declaration with no surgical requirement.

Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015. Marriages performed abroad are registered by notaries and registrars under a National Registry memo, and a couple presenting a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office obtains the same visa, healthcare, inheritance and pension rights as a heterosexual spouse.

The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree imposes procedural obligations on government institutions for LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and in the treatment of victims of armed conflict. A May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. Court judgments from 2004 and 2011 protect entry to public and commercial premises against police and private security.

For trans detainees, a 2011 Constitutional Court ruling permits a prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a later court ruling addressed the treatment of trans detainees more broadly.

Economic discrimination persists: in Caquetá, trans women are limited mainly to hairdressing or sex work, and armed groups there publish lists naming people as targets. Organised threats have forced at least one trans woman to flee her town twice.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports any legal provision, court decision, police action, killing, threat campaign or administrative measure specific to the department of Boyacá. The department's record is unresolved rather than clear.

Whether the national notary route, the 2016 Ministry of Interior decree and the May 2018 executive decree are implemented in practice by Boyacá authorities is not sourced here. Implementation of the national identification markers within the department is likewise not documented in the inventory.

Hate-crime sentencing, police training on gender-based violence and the availability of shelters or trans-specific services in Boyacá are not addressed by the available sources. The causes of the miller/ Millerey killing remain unresolved in the record: police interrogated local residents and, as of the reporting, no arrest had been made.

Whether armed-group flyer campaigns of the kind recorded in Guajira and Caquetá operate in Boyacá is not established. The inventory contains no evidence either for their presence or for their absence.
